evidence.label: Topological triviality of mu-constant families of surface singularities

headline: A claimed proof that surface singularities with a constant Milnor number keep the same topology along a family.
scope: The claim covers one-parameter holomorphic families of isolated singularities of functions of three complex variables.
plain: A singular point of a surface is a spot where it is not smooth, like the tip of a cone. The Milnor number is a whole number that measures how complicated such a point is. The μ-constant problem asks whether keeping this number fixed keeps the shape fixed. It was solved long ago in every dimension except surfaces. This paper claims to solve the surface case: the functions stay the same up to continuous changes of coordinates.
doesNot: This does not give smooth or Whitney-regular coordinate changes, and it says nothing about families with several parameters.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Lê Dũng Tráng and C. P. Ramanujam, every dimension except surfaces
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims a positive answer to the one dimension left open by Lê and Ramanujam's 1976 theorem.

explanation:
Take the function f(x, y, z) = x² + y² + z³ of three complex variables. Its zero set is a surface with one bad point at the origin, called a singularity. There all three partial derivatives, 2x, 2y and 3z², vanish together. The Milnor number μ measures how degenerate that point is. It counts the monomials left after setting x, y and z² to zero. Only 1 and z survive, so μ = 2. Cut a nearby smooth level, such as f = 0.01, inside a small ball. Milnor showed it has the shape of μ spheres joined at one point[1].

Now let the function move with a parameter t. The family x² + y² + z³ + tz² does not keep μ fixed. For t ≠ 0 its z-derivative is z(3z + 2t), which vanishes only simply at z = 0. So μ drops to 1 there. The family x² + y² + z³ + tz⁴ keeps μ = 2 for every t. Near the origin its z-derivative is z² times 3 + 4tz, a factor close to 3.

The μ-constant problem asks whether a constant μ forces the topology to stay the same. The precise form is topological right-triviality[2]. A homeomorphism is a continuous map with a continuous inverse. Right-triviality asks for homeomorphisms φ_t fixing the origin with f_t(φ_t(x)) = f_0(x). The maps and their inverses must also vary continuously with t together.

Lê Dũng Tráng and C. P. Ramanujam proved constant topological type in 1976 for hypersurfaces of every dimension except two[4]. Their method links nearby smooth levels through a cobordism, a space whose boundary is the two shapes. In higher dimensions, the h-cobordism theorem turns that link into a product. Complex dimension two is exactly where that step fails[5]. Outside dimension two, Timourian and King later proved full triviality of the functions themselves[6]. Teissier, Briançon and Speder tied a stronger condition, Whitney regularity, to constancy of a longer list of Milnor numbers. Briançon and Speder also found families that are topologically trivial but not Whitney regular[7]. So a proof from μ alone cannot lean on Whitney regularity. In 2024, Fernández de Bobadilla and Pełka proved that constant μ keeps the multiplicity constant[8].

This paper claims a positive answer in the surface case[9,3]. The dependence on t may be any holomorphic one, meaning given by convergent power series[10]. The main obstacle is numerical. Some singularities belong to a milder class called log canonical. For the others, the paper must show that Wahl's invariant β stays constant, using μ alone[11]. That invariant is read from a resolution, which replaces the bad point by smooth curves.

The proof rests on a cancellation of Euler characteristics[12]. An Euler characteristic is a count like vertices minus edges plus faces. Constant μ keeps one such count fixed on the surfaces of the family[13]. A comparison then writes zero as a sum of counts for extra surfaces plus a correction term. A theorem of Greuel and Steenbrink makes that correction never negative[14]. Langer's form of the Bogomolov–Miyaoka–Yau inequality supplies the opposite sign[15]. So every extra square term must vanish, and β stays constant[16].

Okuma's theorem then gives a resolution of all the surfaces at once, after a finite cover of the disk[17]. The paper lifts the motion in t to these resolved surfaces. The lifts push down to the zero sets and extend to nearby levels, keeping f fixed[18]. Log-canonical singularities and double points are handled by a separate argument[19].

How sure is this? There is no Lean scope note for this result, so no computer proof checker has tested it. The paper claims to prove the full surface case. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. It is a single long paper with no Lean scope note. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A point where a surface fails to be smooth, like the tip of a cone.
A whole number measuring how degenerate an isolated singular point of a function is.
A continuous map with a continuous inverse.
A family whose functions all match the first one after continuous changes of coordinates that vary continuously with the parameter.
A stronger, geometric form of a family staying the same along its singular points.
A smooth surface that maps onto a singular one, replacing each bad point by smooth curves.
A count of a shape's pieces, like vertices minus edges plus faces.

claims.text: The Milnor fiber has the homotopy type of a bouquet of spheres, one for each unit of the Milnor number.
claims.sourceLine: fiber has the homotopy type of a bouquet of spheres, with one sphere for each unit of the Milnor number
claims.sourceQuote: The Milnor number measures the topology of a nearby smooth level of an isolated hypersurface singularity: its Milnor fiber has the homotopy type of a bouquet of spheres, with one sphere for each unit of the Milnor number \cite[Theorems~6.5 and~7.2]{Milnor1968}; the analytic formulation in terms of the Jacobian algebra is recalled in \cite[Section~1, Theorem~1.5]{LeRamanujam1976}.

claims.text: Topological right-triviality: a homeomorphism germ preserving the parameter and origin section identifies each function with the central one.
claims.sourceLine: if a homeomorphism germ of the ambient family, preserving the parameter and the origin section, identifies each defining function with the central one.
claims.sourceQuote: The family is \emph{topologically right-trivial} if a homeomorphism germ of the ambient family, preserving the parameter and the origin section, identifies each defining function with the central one.

claims.text: Main theorem: for a μ-constant family there is a homeomorphism germ Φ with f_t(φ_t(x)) = f_0(x), jointly continuous with its inverse.
